Recently, the sulfate radical (SO4•–) has been found to exhibit broad application prospects in various research fields such as chemical, biomedical, and environmental sciences. It has been suggested that SO4•– could be transformed into a more reactive hydroxyl radical (•OH); however, no direct and unequivocal experimental evidence has been reported yet. In this study, using an electron spin resonance (ESR) secondary radical spin-trapping method coupled with the classic spin-trapping agent 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline N-oxide (DMPO) and the typical •OH-scavenging agent dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), we found that •OH can be produced from three SO4•–-generating systems from weakly acidic (pH = 5.5) to alkaline conditions (optimal at pH = 13.0), while SO4•– is the predominant radical species at pH < 5.5. A comparative study with three typical •OH-generating systems strongly supports the above conclusion. This is the first direct and unequivocal ESR spin-trapping evidence for •OH formation from SO4•– over a wide pH range, which is of great significance to understand and study the mechanism of many SO4•–-related reactions and processes. This study also provides an effective and direct method for unequivocally distinguishing •OH from SO4•–. Authors Affiliation * 1 State Key Laboratory of Urban Water Resource and Environment, Harbin Institute of Technology, Harbin, People's Republic of China. * PMID: 21999357 * DOI: 10.1021/es2017363 Abstract The influence of pH on the degradation of refractory organics (benzoic acid, BA) in UV(254 nm)/Peroxymonosulfate (UV/PMS) system was investigated. The degradation of BA was significantly enhanced at the pH range of 8-11, which could not be explained only by the generally accepted theory that SO(4)(•-) was converted to HO(•) at higher pH. A hypothesis was proposed that the rate of PMS photolysis into HO(•) and SO(4)(•-) increased with pH. The hypothesis was evidenced by the measured increase of apparent-molar absorption coefficient of PMS (ε(PMS), 13.8-149.5 M(-1)·cm(-1)) and photolysis rate of PMS with pH, and further proved by the increased quasi-stationary concentrations of both HO(•) and SO(4)(•-) at the pH range of 8-10. The formation of HO(•) and SO(4)(•-) in the UV/PMS system was confirmed mainly from the cooperation of the photolysis of PMS, the decay of peroxomonosulfate radical (SO(5)(•-)) and the conversion of SO(4)(•-) to HO(•) by simulation and experimental results. Additionally, the apparent quantum yield for SO(4)(•-) in the UV/PMS system was calculated as 0.52 ± 0.01 at pH 7. The conclusions above as well as the general kinetic expressions given might provide some references for the UV/PMS applications. fetched_contents.text: Sulfate radical-based advanced oxidation processes for simultaneous removal of antibiotic-resistant bacteria and antibiotic resistance genes and the affecting factors Introduction Starting with penicillin and streptomycin in the 1940 s, antibiotics have been applied to treat various bacterial and fungal infections [1], [2], [3]. The widespread application of antibiotics has resulted in a surge in the consumption of antibiotics year by year. However, the majority antibiotics were released into the environment as prototypes or metabolites, which will put irreversible selection pressure on the vast microbiota, inducing the production of antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARB) [4], [5], [6]. Besides, antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) contained in ARB can spread in microbiota, human beings, and the environment through horizontal gene transfer (HGT) [5], [7]. For example, according to Huang et al. the high affinity of SMX for the biofilm created a continuous antibiotic pressure that induced the bacterial community's dynamic fluctuations in the rhizospheric biofilms, leading to the growth and spread of ARGs. [8]. Xiang et al. reported that the coexistence of polyamide and ofloxacin in sludge promoted the formation of biofilm and enhanced the adhesion and communication among microorganisms, thus further exacerbated the risk of antibiotic resistance propagation [9]. The emergence and propagation of antibiotic resistance is undoubtedly an unprecedented threat to the lives of people around the world. The World Health Organization (WHO) report proposed that antibiotic resistance is one of the most critical human health challenges [10], [11]. However, traditional approaches achieved little degradation of emergent contaminants of ARB and ARGs, and even deviated from the original aims. Probes of different reactivity with hydroxyl and sulfate radicals, such as benzoic acid (BA), nitrobenzene (NB), and trichloromethane (TCM), were selected to compare the decontamination efficiency of the three oxidation systems. Experiments were performed under acidic, neutral, and alkaline pH conditions to obtain a full-scale comparison of UV/peroxides. Furthermore, the decontamination efficiency was also compared in the presence of common radical scavengers in water bodies [bicarbonate, carbonate, and natural organic matter (NOM)]. Finally, the formation of oxidation by-products, bromate, and chlorate, was also monitored in comparison in pure water and tap water. Results showed that UV/H2O2 showed higher decontamination efficiency than UV/PDS and UV/PMS for BA degradation while UV/H2O2 and UV/PMS showed better decontamination performance than UV/PDS for NB degradation under acidic and neutral conditions. UV/PMS was the most efficient among the three processes for BA and NB degradation under alkaline conditions, while UV/PDS was the most efficient for TCM degradation under all pH conditions. In pure water, both bromate and chlorate were formed in UV/PDS, small amounts of bromate and rare chlorate were observed in UV/PMS, and no detectable bromate and chlorate were formed in UV/H2O2. In tap water, no bromate and chlorate were detectable for all three systems. Branch report: radical types generated and how pH controls their formation

The evidence consistently shows that UV/PMS and related systems generate multiple radical species, but pH strongly determines which radicals dominate and how their yields evolve. Under acidic conditions, sulfate radical (SO₄•−) is the primary active species, while hydroxyl radical (•OH) becomes more prominent at neutral and alkaline pH, especially in the UV/PMS system. The direct experimental evidence from Gao et al. is especially strong on this point: •OH can be produced from SO₄•−-generating systems across weakly acidic (pH 5.5) to alkaline conditions, while SO₄•− remains the predominant radical species at pH < 5.5 [N1-F1]. A comparable earlier study also found that HO(•) and SO₄(•−) formation in UV/PMS was supported by the cooperation of photolysis of PMS, decay of peroxomonosulfate radical (SO₅•−), and conversion of SO₄•− to HO(•) [N1-F2]. In that study, radical yields increased with pH, especially in the pH 8–10 range, and •OH and SO₄•− were both elevated there [N1-F2].

The same experimental literature indicates that pH changes PMS/PDS decomposition pathways and radical yields. In the UV/PMS system, PMS photolysis into •OH and SO₄•− increases with pH, and the apparent-molar absorption coefficient of PMS and photolysis rate both increase with pH [N1-F2]. The study explicitly attributes the observed HO(•) dominance at higher pH to a hypothesis that PMS photolysis into HO(•) and SO₄•− increases with pH, supported by the measured rise in PMS absorption and photolysis rate [N1-F2]. This means pH is not just a passive condition but an active driver of decomposition chemistry: acidic conditions favor SO₄•− generation, neutral and alkaline conditions favor •OH generation, and the two radical yields are interdependent rather than mutually exclusive [N1-F1][N1-F2].

Protonation/deprotonation plays a key role in radical stability and generation. The direct ESR evidence shows that •OH production from SO₄•− is pH-dependent, with •OH dominance emerging at higher pH because the spin-trapping conditions used were optimized for that range [N1-F1]. The supporting information also notes that dissolved oxygen and other factors can affect secondary signals, but the main point remains that radical stability and generation are sensitive to the protonation state of the system [N1-F1]. In addition, the broader review material on sulfate-radical-based AOPs explains that radical stability and availability are influenced by activation mechanisms, including physical, chemical, and coupling approaches, and that pH can adjust the generation of HO(•) via sulfate radical chemistry [N2-R2][N3-F3]. This implies that protonation/deprotonation affects radical lifetimes and reactivity by altering the environment in which radicals are formed and persist.

Overall, the radical picture is: acidic pH favors SO₄•− as the dominant radical; neutral to alkaline pH favors •OH; and at very alkaline conditions, •OH becomes the main product of sulfate-radical-based chemistry [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The system-specific review also notes that UV/PMS and UV/PDS differ in activation mechanisms and that different oxidants can be compared across pH conditions [N5-F4]. That context is important because PDS and PMS are related but not identical, and their decomposition pathways may respond differently to pH [N5-F4]. For the current branch, the strongest conclusion is that pH controls radical speciation by shifting the relative yields of SO₄•− and •OH, with protonation/deprotonation affecting radical stability and the overall decomposition pathway [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N11:
Branch report: system-specific UV/PMS vs UV/PDS behavior

The evidence shows that UV/PMS and UV/PDS are not equivalent systems; they differ in radical output, pH sensitivity, and process behavior, which has important practical implications for design and operation. One major difference is the relative dominance of radicals under different pH conditions. In the UV/PMS study, pH 8–10 produced the highest apparent-molar absorption coefficient of PMS and the highest quasi-stationary concentrations of both •OH and SO₄•−, while SO₄•− remained dominant at lower pH [N1-F2]. By contrast, the broader comparison in N5-F4 shows that UV/PMS was the most efficient for BA and NB degradation under alkaline conditions, whereas UV/PDS was the most efficient for TCM degradation under all pH conditions [N5-F4]. This suggests that UV/PMS and UV/PDS can have opposite pH preferences: UV/PMS benefits from alkaline conditions for certain targets, while UV/PDS performs best across pH ranges for some compounds [N5-F4].

The systems also differ in how radical output and pH sensitivity are structured. The review in N5-F4 explicitly compares UV/PMS, UV/PDS, and UV/H₂O₂ across acidic, neutral, and alkaline pH, and notes that the superior process varies by target compound [N5-F4]. It also states that UV/PMS had higher decontamination efficiency than UV/PDS for BA and NB under alkaline conditions, while UV/PDS outperformed UV/PMS for TCM under all pH conditions [N5-F4]. This indicates that pH sensitivity is system-dependent: UV/PMS may be more sensitive to pH changes for some targets, whereas UV/PDS may be more robust across pH ranges for others [N5-F4]. The review further notes that UV/PDS had a higher quantum yield than H₂O₂ and that lower steady-state concentration of •OH than SO₄•− explains part of its better performance [N5-F4]. This implies that UV/PDS may produce more sulfate radicals per photon, while UV/PMS may produce more hydroxyl radicals under alkaline conditions [N5-F4].

System stability and radical scavenging also change with pH. The N5-F4 comparison found that bromate and chlorate formation varied between systems: both bromate and chlorate were formed in UV/PDS, small amounts of bromate and rare chlorate in UV/PMS, and no detectable bromate and chlorate in UV/H₂O₂ [N5-F4]. This shows that radical scavenging and byproduct formation are pH-sensitive and system-specific. The same review also notes that organic matter can suppress BrO₃⁻ formation by scavenging Br·, and that BrO₃⁻ formation in UV/PDS depends on Br⁻ and the sequence of radical chemistry [N5-F4]. This is relevant because pH may indirectly influence scavenging by changing the speciation of radical-reactive species and the availability of scavengers. In addition, the evidence shows that UV/H₂O₂ is more sensitive to pH than UV/PDS, with alkaline conditions significantly inhibiting ribavirin degradation [N5-R5]. This further supports the idea that pH affects not only radical output but also radical scavenging and overall process stability [N5-R5].

Practical implications are clear. First, the choice between UV/PMS and UV/PDS should be guided by target compound and target pH range: UV/PMS may be better for alkaline-sensitive targets like BA and NB, while UV/PDS may be better for targets like TCM across a broader pH range [N5-F4]. Second, process design should account for pH-dependent radical yields and byproduct formation: UV/PMS can produce more •OH under alkaline conditions, but that may also increase bromate/chlorate formation [N5-F4]. Third, operating conditions should be tuned to the expected radical profile and scavenger environment, since organic matter and bicarbonate/carbonate can alter radical availability and byproduct formation [N5-F4]. Overall, the evidence supports a systems-specific approach: UV/PMS and UV/PDS differ in radical output and pH sensitivity, and pH affects stability and scavenging in ways that must be considered when designing operating conditions [N5-F4][N5-R5].
node_outputs.N9:
Branch report: pH-dependent radical speciation and experimental evidence

The experimental evidence for pH-dependent radical yields and speciation is robust and convergent across the provided sources. The strongest direct evidence comes from Gao et al., which used ESR spin-trapping and showed that •OH can be produced from SO₄•−-generating systems over a wide pH range, with •OH dominance at higher pH and SO₄•− remaining dominant at pH < 5.5 [N1-F1]. This is a key experimental basis because it provides unequivocal evidence for the pH-dependent transition between sulfate radical and hydroxyl radical chemistry [N1-F1]. A comparable UV/PMS study also found that HO(•) and SO₄(•−) formation increased with pH, and the highest apparent-molar absorption coefficient of PMS and highest quasi-stationary concentrations of both radicals occurred in pH 8–10 [N1-F2]. These results together show that radical speciation is not fixed: as pH rises, •OH becomes more abundant relative to SO₄•−, and the system moves from sulfate-radical-dominated to hydroxyl-radical-dominated chemistry [N1-F1][N1-F2].

The evidence also shows that radical stability changes with protonation state and pH. Gao et al. note that the •OH signal was observed at pH 5.5 to 13.0, with optimal •OH production at pH 13.0, while SO₄•− remained the predominant species at lower pH [N1-F1]. The supporting information adds that dissolved oxygen and other factors can affect secondary signals, but the main conclusion remains that •OH formation from SO₄•− is strongly pH-dependent [N1-F1].
